client:
I've been really struggling with my new job at the marketing agency. Everyone else seems to know exactly what they're doing, and I feel like I'm constantly playing catch-up. I lie awake at night worrying that they'll realize I'm not qualified and fire me. 

Honestly, I'm not sure talking about it will help - the problem is that I just don't have the experience the others do.
therapist: I hear how overwhelming this feels for you right now, with your voice sounding tense and rushed as you describe this struggle. That worry about not measuring up sounds exhausting, and I'm noticing how much it's weighing on you both day and night. Would you be open to exploring what evidence you have about your actual performance versus these fears?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client:
I don't know...when you ask for evidence, all I can think about are the times I messed up at work last month. My boss hasn't said anything negative, but I keep waiting for the other shoe to drop. It's like my brain only remembers the mistakes, not the things I did right. 

The idea of looking at evidence makes me anxious because what if I find proof that I really am failing? I've been having trouble sleeping because I keep replaying every little error in my head.
therapist:
Your voice sounds quite strained as you describe this, and I can hear how much this pattern of focusing on mistakes is distressing you. It's understandable to feel this anxious when your mind keeps highlighting the negatives - that's what anxious minds tend to do. 

Would it help to gently examine whether there might be other explanations for why your boss hasn't said anything, besides waiting to fire you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess it’s possible that my boss hasn’t said anything because they’re busy or just haven’t noticed the mistake, but it’s hard to believe that. My mind keeps going back to the worst-case scenario, and it feels like I’m just waiting for the other shoe to drop. Even if there are other explanations, I still feel so guilty and anxious about it—like I messed up something important and it’s only a matter of time before it’s addressed.
therapist:
Your voice sounds heavy with worry as you share this, and I can hear how stuck you feel in these anxious thought patterns. It's understandable to feel this guilt and anticipation when your mind keeps focusing on that worst-case scenario.

vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I have handled challenges before, but those situations feel different. This time, it’s like no matter what I do, I can’t shake the feeling that I’ll mess it all up. It’s not just about the work itself—it’s the fear of letting everyone down and being judged for it. Even when I’ve succeeded in the past, it doesn’t feel like it counts because this feels so much bigger.
therapist:

client:
It's different because before, I could see an end point - like studying for an exam or preparing for a presentation. But now it's just this constant background dread about everything. I wake up with it and go to bed with it, and I can't remember what it feels like to just... breathe normally anymore. 

And the worst part is I know logically that I've handled tough situations before, but that knowledge doesn't help when my chest gets tight in the grocery store for no reason. It makes me feel weak, like I should be stronger than this.
therapist:

therapist:

client:
